strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching failure: residual misalignment that seam selection alone cannot resolve. Repairing patches around problematic seam segments is a useful, targeted approach.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets. Figures 1, 7, 10, and 11 show convincing examples of improved continuity around curbs, stairs, and other structures.

The user study provides some independent perceptual support: the proposed method receives 108 of 160 first-place votes on the eight selected examples. CPU timing comparisons also demonstrate advantages over expensive iterative seam estimation in difficult cases.

The pipeline is understandable at a high level, credits its principal components and public data sources, and reports several implementation parameters. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 usefully explain failures under widespread misalignment and large residual displacement.
weaknesses: The central warp modification is insufficiently specified. Section 3.4 writes f(V_i(p_j)), but Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid whose input is subsequently described as a spatial coordinate. The exact modified two-dimensional displacement, orientation selection, and treatment of patch boundaries remain unclear. Fixing boundary labels in Section 3.5 does not itself ensure continuity of the warped image. These details are essential to reproducing the main contribution.

The contribution is primarily an integration of established seam evaluation, SIFT flow, sigmoid weighting, and graph-cut composition. This can be valuable, but the experiments do not isolate the benefit of the proposed design. Beyond the single-patch illustration in Figure 4, there are no controlled quantitative ablations of patch selection, flow modification, or boundary constraints. Only one initial alignment and seam-cutting combination is tested, leaving the claimed general compatibility unverified.

Quantitative comparisons are restricted to seam-cutting methods [16] and [17], which retain the initial alignment. Comparisons against methods that also refine alignment are particularly important for this contribution. SEAGULL [18] and method [26] receive only limited qualitative comparison, while the cited residual-warping approach [12] is not evaluated. Consequently, the evidence establishes improvement over fixed-alignment seam selection more convincingly than advancement over competing parallax-handling methods.

The principal metric, Equation (5), measures essentially the same local SSIM disagreement used to identify repair regions. It does not assess geometric distortion or content preservation elsewhere in the mosaic, and the manuscript itself identifies a disagreement with visual quality. The user study helps, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples, unspecified presentation randomization, and lack of per-image results limit generalization to the full evaluation set.

The claim that the method can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption exceeds its demonstrated scope. Sections 3.3–3.4 still require predominantly successful initial alignment and small local parallax. Moreover, max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts a uniformly high-error seam as plausible, and the algorithm provides no explicit post-repair acceptance check supporting the assertion that false-positive repairs cannot worsen results. The acknowledged limitations support a narrower contribution in local residual repair, whose robustness needs stronger validation.
